title: Replace a server's CR2032 system battery in its latched socket
instruction: Replace the server's system battery and put the spent cell in the disposal tray.
context: Done by data-centre and field-service technicians (computer, ATM and office machine repairers, O*NET 49-2011; data-centre technicians). Every rack server keeps its clock and firmware settings on a CR2032 cell in a latched board socket, and replacing it is a standard procedure in Dell PowerEdge (KB 000234357), Lenovo ThinkSystem (SR650: press the battery clip and lift the cell out; SR630 V3: + side up, tilt it in, press until it clicks) and HPE ProLiant guides; fleets of millions of servers make it routine maintenance robots must do to run data centres. What goes wrong: a lithium cell dropped on the board or into the chassis (short, fire), a forced socket, a cell not under the hook or a clip not caught. Hard because a 20 x 3.2 mm, 3 g disc lying flat can't be pinched until the latch is squeezed back and the contact spring tips it up, and the new cell must go under a 0.8 mm hook and be pressed flat over the latch.
setup: Station table top z=0.7475 m; x forward, y left; arm bases (0,+-0.305). Real size, metres. Chassis tray (1.0 mm steel, fixed): floor x 0.060-0.270, y -0.090-0.090 with 12 mm flanges; four 6 mm M3 brass standoffs. System-board section (FR-4 1.6 mm, fixed) x 0.085-0.245, y -0.075-0.075, top z 0.7561, with a PCIe x16 slot body (89 x 7.5 x 11.25 mm) centred (0.120, 0). CR2032 socket (fixed base) centred (0.150, 0) on the board: seat, fixed hook on the -x side (lip underside 4.5 mm above the board, 0.8 mm over the cell edge), four 3 mm locating posts, housing wall 8.6 mm high behind a spring-steel latch on the +x side (slides 0-1.5 mm outward; 400 N/m, 0.4 N closed, 1.0 N open; 45-degree lead-in; lip 0.8 mm over the cell edge; 8.6 mm upturned release tab) and a sprung negative contact under the cell (rises 0-3 mm; 0.8 N on a latched cell, 0.2 N at full lift). Spent CR2032 (20.0 x 3.2 mm, 3.0 g, nickel-plated steel, + up) latched in it, centre z 0.7590. New CR2032, + up, on a staging boss (40 x 40 x 3 mm plate, 12 mm dia x 8 mm boss) at (0.150, 0.125), centre z 0.7601. Disposal tray (ESD, 60 x 50 x 20 mm, 2 mm walls, fixed) at (0.150, -0.130). Every dimension and calibration: README.
scoring: End state, from object poses (in a real trial: a top photo and a side photo with a scale, plus video for drops). Sub-goal A (0.25): the spent cell lies inside the disposal tray's walls (bounding box within 2 mm of the inner faces, on the floor, below the rim), released and still. Sub-goal B (0.75): the new cell is latched: centre within 1.5 mm of the socket centre in plan and 0.8 mm of the latched height (2.9 mm above the board), tilt 5 degrees or less with the + face up, and the latch back within 0.5 mm of closed (its lip over the cell edge), released and still for 1 s. A new cell in the socket but not latched (centre within 5 mm, lowest point 2.5 mm or less above the board, + up within 45 degrees, released and still) earns 0.25 instead of 0.75. Score = A + B (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0). Released: both grippers' centre points at least 30 mm from the cell's bounding box. Still: the cell moved under 0.5 mm and turned under 1 degree over the last 1 s. Polarity is judged at the end only. Score 0 for the rest of the trial if a released cell ever lies on the board or chassis floor outside the socket (centre over the chassis, more than 13 mm from the socket centre, lowest point within 12 mm of the board top: a short-circuit hazard on a live board) or falls more than 30 mm below the table top. Full score ends the trial after 1 s.
reset_notes: Latch the spent cell + up in the socket, put a new CR2032 + up on the staging boss, empty the disposal tray. Socket, board, chassis, stand and tray are fixed. In a real trial use a dummy board (no power) and insulate spent cells before disposal.
fidelity: Socket built from boxes and one convex extruded lead-in; the bent spring-steel latch is a sprung slide and the leaf contact a sprung plunger, with forces (latch 0.4-1.0 N, contact 0.8 N) kept inside the simulated arm's push budget; real latches may be stiffer. Cells are rigid discs; no electrical contact is simulated (polarity judged from orientation). Board is a section with one neighbouring connector. Stillness is judged from pose over 1 s. Dream-1 sees a 20 mm cell as a few pixels.
